criteria_results.title: Factual Background: Section 7.3 Restriction on Use of Background IP

This satisfies all elements of the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Factual Background: LumiSense 400 Product and Its Substrate
criteria_results.reasoning: The counterclaim extensively describes the LumiSense 400 substrate matching SensorCore™ architecture. Paragraphs 47-52 detail the teardown analysis findings, including: exactly 14 copper-pillar micro-bump interconnect layers (¶51(a)), measured micro-bump pitch of 44.8μm ± 0.3μm matching SensorCore's 45μm specification (¶51(b)), radial-array thermal via pattern with 93% positional correspondence (¶51(c)), identical Ti/Cu/Ni under-bump metallization stack (¶51(d)), and distinctive non-functional design features like 'cross-hair with quadrant notch' registration marks and 'dog-leg' routing paths (¶51(e-f)). These specific technical similarities are clearly and thoroughly alleged.

criteria_results.title: Factual Background: Dr. Ayers Expert Teardown Conclusions
criteria_results.reasoning: Paragraphs 50-52 of the counterclaim detail Dr. Franklin Ayers of Ridgeline Technical Consulting LLC performing a teardown and comparative analysis of the LumiSense 400. Paragraph 52 explicitly states his conclusion that the LumiSense 400 substrate is 'substantially derived from Vantage's SensorCore™ architecture' and that 'the probability of independent development of all the matching features is less than one in ten million.' This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Factual Background: Bellingham Email (May 15, 2022) — Smoking Gun

It also includes Bellingham's statement that 'Our coating process is already 18 months ahead of schedule for internal commercialization --- we don't need their sensor expertise, but their SensorCore designs would leapfrog our LiDAR sensor program by 2+ years.' Both the date and the substance (real value = substrate tech, coating process ahead of schedule) are present.

criteria_results.title: Factual Background: DeLuca Reply Email (May 16, 2022) — Smoking Gun
criteria_results.reasoning: Paragraphs 25 and 26 of the counterclaim explicitly quote and reference Martin DeLuca's reply email dated May 16, 2022, including the exact language 'Agreed. Let's keep Meridian going long enough to extract what we need' and his direction that 'Vasquez gets full portal access from day one.' The date, the substance, and the key quotes are all present.

This directly satisfies the criterion requiring the $14.2M revenue figure tied to the March 1, 2024 commercial launch through June 30, 2024.

criteria_results.title: Factual Background: Northfield Aerospace Lost Contract ($8.7M)
criteria_results.reasoning: The document explicitly references the Northfield Aerospace Solutions lost contract in multiple places. criteria_results.title: Count: Breach of JDA — M2 Partial/Late Delivery (ISSUE_004a)
criteria_results.reasoning: Count I (Breach of Contract: JDA) at paragraph 58(a) specifically alleges that Lumenara breached the JDA by 'failing to deliver fifty conforming prototype assemblies by March 31, 2023 (M2), in breach of Sections 2.3(b) and 6.2(b) and Exhibit A.' Paragraph 39(a) provides the specific factual detail: Lumenara delivered only 28 units (56% of required quantity), 22 days late (April 22, 2023), and never delivered the remaining 22 units. This satisfies the criterion requiring specific allegation of M2 partial/late delivery as a breach of the JDA.

criteria_results.title: Count: Breach of JDA — M3 Non-Delivery (ISSUE_004b)
criteria_results.reasoning: Count I (Breach of Contract: JDA) at paragraph 58(b) specifically alleges that Lumenara breached the JDA by 'failing to deliver a complete MIL-STD-810H data package by September 30, 2023 (M3), in breach of Sections 2.3(c) and 6.2(c) and Exhibit A.' Paragraph 39(b) provides detailed factual allegations about M3 non-delivery, noting Lumenara delivered nothing by the deadline and that the partial data it eventually submitted 'shall not constitute achievement of M3.' This is a distinct breach allegation within the breach of JDA count.

criteria_results.title: Count: Breach of JDA — M4 Non-Delivery (ISSUE_004c)
criteria_results.reasoning: Count I (Breach of Contract: JDA) at paragraph 58 explicitly alleges that Lumenara breached the JDA by '(c) failing to deliver production-ready coating process documentation by March 31, 2024 (M4), in breach of Sections 2.3(d) and 6.2(d) and Exhibit A.' This is a distinct, specifically identified breach allegation for M4 non-delivery within the breach of JDA count. Paragraph 39(c) also provides detailed factual support: 'M4. Lumenara delivered no production-ready coating process documentation by March 31, 2024. It has delivered none since.' The M4 non-delivery is clearly alleged as a distinct breach within the breach of JDA claim.

criteria_results.title: Count: Breach of JDA — Unauthorized Use of Background IP (ISSUE_004d)
criteria_results.reasoning: Count II (Breach of Contract: Joint Development Agreement — Background IP, Use, and Confidentiality Restrictions) explicitly alleges that Lumenara used Vantage's Background IP (SensorCore™ designs) for purposes other than the Project without signed written consent in violation of Section 7.3(a), incorporated it into the LumiSense 400 in violation of Section 7.3(b)(i), and used it to develop a competing product in violation of Section 7.3(b)(v). This directly satisfies the criterion requiring a breach of JDA count specifically alleging unauthorized use of Vantage's Background IP outside the scope of Project Meridian in violation of Section 7.3.

criteria_results.title: Count: DTSA Misappropriation Counterclaim (ISSUE_003)
criteria_results.reasoning: COUNT IV is explicitly titled 'Misappropriation of Trade Secrets: Defend Trade Secrets Act, 18 U.S.C. § 1836 et seq.' and cites 18 U.S.C. § 1836, § 1839(3), § 1839(5), § 1839(6), and § 1836(b)(3) throughout. It alleges Lumenara misappropriated Vantage's SensorCore™ trade secrets. This is a separate, clearly labeled federal DTSA count distinct from the Texas UTSA count (COUNT V).

criteria_results.title: DTSA Count: Existence of Trade Secret Alleged
criteria_results.reasoning: COUNT IV (DTSA) explicitly alleges in paragraphs 77-78 that the SensorCore™ Trade Secrets are trade secrets under 18 U.S.C. § 1839(3), that they derive independent economic value from not being generally known or readily ascertainable, and that Vantage took reasonable measures to keep them secret (referencing paragraph 17, which details the MNDA, file markings, portal access controls, IP whitelisting, activity logging, and limited authorized users). Both required elements — independent economic value from secrecy and reasonable protective measures — are clearly alleged in the DTSA count.

criteria_results.title: DTSA Count: Misappropriation by Improper Means or Breach of Duty
criteria_results.reasoning: Count IV (paragraphs 76-84) explicitly alleges misappropriation under the DTSA through two theories: (1) acquisition by improper means—specifically misrepresentation, as Lumenara obtained Portal access by falsely representing good-faith intent while secretly planning to 'extract' Vantage's substrate technology (18 U.S.C. § 1839(6)); and (2) use and disclosure without consent while knowing the trade secrets were acquired under circumstances giving rise to a duty to maintain secrecy (the MNDA and JDA). The count also details Vasquez's unauthorized downloads and the commercial exploitation in the LumiSense 400. All required misappropriation elements are clearly alleged.

criteria_results.title: DTSA Count: Interstate Commerce Nexus
criteria_results.reasoning: Paragraph 79 of Count IV explicitly addresses the interstate commerce nexus: 'The SensorCore™ Trade Secrets relate to products used in, or intended for use in, interstate and foreign commerce, including Vantage's sensor modules sold to aerospace and defense customers nationwide and the LumiSense 400, which Lumenara sells across state lines.' This directly satisfies the DTSA requirement under 18 U.S.C. § 1839(3) and the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Count: Breach of MNDA (ISSUE_006)
criteria_results.reasoning: Count III of the counterclaim is explicitly titled 'Breach of Contract: Mutual Non-Disclosure Agreement' and alleges that Lumenara breached the MNDA by using Vantage's Confidential Information (including the SensorCore™ design package) for purposes other than the permitted Purpose, specifically including the development, manufacture, marketing, and sale of the LumiSense 400, in violation of Section 3.2 of the MNDA. This directly satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Count: Fraudulent Inducement (ISSUE_001)
criteria_results.reasoning: COUNT VI is explicitly titled 'Fraudulent Inducement' and alleges that Lumenara misrepresented its intent to genuinely collaborate (Section 9.3 representations) when its actual intent was to extract Vantage's SensorCore substrate technology, as evidenced by the pre-signing emails. The count identifies the specific misrepresentations, their falsity, Lumenara's knowledge, intent to induce reliance, actual reliance, and resulting injury. This fully satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Fraudulent Inducement: Rule 9(b) Specificity — Who
criteria_results.reasoning: Count VI (Fraudulent Inducement) specifically identifies Martin DeLuca (Lumenara's CEO) as the person who made the written representations in Section 9.3 of the JDA on June 1, 2022, and Craig Bellingham (Lumenara's Program Manager) as the person who sent the May 15, 2022 email outlining the scheme. The count also references Dr. Kevin Zhao as part of the 'close-hold' group. The allegations identify who made the misrepresentations (DeLuca executing the JDA), who directed the scheme (DeLuca and Bellingham via the May 2022 emails), and the specific dates and content of their communications. This satisfies Rule 9(b)'s particularity requirement for identifying the specific persons involved in the fraudulent inducement.

criteria_results.title: Fraudulent Inducement: Rule 9(b) Specificity — What
criteria_results.reasoning: Count VI (Fraudulent Inducement) at paragraphs 91-99 specifically identifies the misrepresentations: (a) that Lumenara 'is entering into this Agreement in good faith and with the genuine intent to perform its obligations hereunder and to devote the resources and efforts necessary to achieve the Project Objective'; and (b) that Lumenara 'has no present intention or plan to use the collaboration contemplated by this Agreement for any purpose other than the Project.' The count further explains that these representations were false because Lumenara's CEO and Program Manager had already agreed to 'extract' Vantage's substrate technology and only perform early milestones to maintain the appearance of good faith. The specific nature of the misrepresentation — that Lumenara falsely represented genuine collaborative intent when it actually intended to extract SensorCore™ technology — is clearly described with particularity including the who (DeLuca), what (Section 9.3 representations), when (June 1, 2022), and the underlying fraudulent intent documented in the May 15-16, 2022 emails.

criteria_results.title: Fraudulent Inducement: Rule 9(b) Specificity — When
criteria_results.reasoning: The fraudulent inducement count (Count VI) explicitly identifies the May 15, 2022 email from Bellingham to DeLuca and the May 16, 2022 reply from DeLuca as establishing pre-JDA fraudulent intent, and identifies June 1, 2022 as the date the misrepresentations were made (when DeLuca executed the JDA containing Section 9.3 representations). Paragraphs 93-96 provide specific dates, speakers, and content of the fraudulent communications, satisfying Rule 9(b)'s particularity requirement for the 'when' element.

criteria_results.title: Fraudulent Inducement: Reliance Alleged
criteria_results.reasoning: Count VI (Fraudulent Inducement) at paragraph 96 explicitly alleges: 'Vantage actually and justifiably relied on Lumenara's representations. Vantage would not have executed the JDA, committed its resources, or uploaded the SensorCore™ design package had it known that Lumenara did not intend to perform and intended to use the collaboration to obtain Vantage's substrate technology.' This directly satisfies the criterion requiring allegation of justifiable reliance and that Vantage would not have entered the JDA or shared its SensorCore™ designs but for the misrepresentations.

criteria_results.title: Count: Patent Infringement (ISSUE_005)
criteria_results.reasoning: COUNT VII of the counterclaim is explicitly titled 'Patent Infringement: U.S. Patent No. 11,234,567 (35 U.S.C. § 271)' and alleges that the LumiSense 400 directly infringes at least claim 1 of the '567 Patent covering the SensorCore™ architecture. The count includes claim mapping, willfulness allegations, and requests for damages and injunctive relief under 35 U.S.C. §§ 283-285.

criteria_results.title: Patent Infringement Count: Patent Number Cited
criteria_results.reasoning: COUNT VII (Patent Infringement) explicitly identifies 'U.S. Patent No. 11,234,567' and refers to it as 'the '567 Patent' throughout the count, including in paragraphs 101, 102, 103, 104, 105, 106, and 107.

criteria_results.title: Patent Infringement Count: Basis for Infringement
criteria_results.reasoning: Count VII (paragraphs 100-107) provides a detailed factual basis for patent infringement. It identifies the specific patent (U.S. Patent No. 11,234,567), recites the claim elements (at least 14 copper-pillar micro-bump interconnect layers, ~45μm micro-bump pitch, radial-array thermal via pattern), and maps each element to the LumiSense 400 using the expert teardown analysis: exactly 14 layers, measured pitch of 44.8μm ± 0.3μm, and a radial-array thermal via pattern. The count also references Dr. Ayers' teardown methodology and findings from paragraph 51, which provide the evidentiary foundation. This goes well beyond a bare assertion of infringement and satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Count: Unjust Enrichment in the Alternative (ISSUE_007)
criteria_results.reasoning: The counterclaim does not include a standalone count for unjust enrichment pleaded in the alternative. While the document references 'unjust enrichment' in the context of the trade secret damages remedies (Counts IV and V, citing 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(B) and Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 134A.004(a)), these references are to a damages measure within the trade secret misappropriation counts, not a separate count for unjust enrichment pleaded in the alternative to the contract claims (e.g., in the event the JDA or MNDA is found unenforceable). There is no count labeled 'Unjust Enrichment' and no language invoking Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(d)(2) or 8(d)(3) to plead unjust enrichment as an alternative to the breach of contract claims. The criterion requires unjust enrichment to be asserted as an alternative claim, which it is not here.

criteria_results.title: Count: Conversion (ISSUE_008)
criteria_results.reasoning: The counterclaim includes seven counts: breach of contract (JDA milestones/representations), breach of contract (Background IP/use/confidentiality), breach of contract (MNDA), misappropriation of trade secrets (DTSA), misappropriation of trade secrets (Texas UTSA), fraudulent inducement, and patent infringement. There is no count for conversion alleging that Lumenara wrongfully exercised dominion and control over Vantage's proprietary SensorCore™ design files by downloading and commercially exploiting them without authorization.

criteria_results.title: TUTSA Preemption Addressed (ISSUE_012)
criteria_results.reasoning: The counterclaim does not assert common-law claims of conversion or unjust enrichment as standalone causes of action. The claims asserted are: breach of JDA, breach of MNDA, DTSA misappropriation, TUTSA misappropriation, fraudulent inducement, and patent infringement. The unjust enrichment concept appears only as a damages measure within the trade secret counts (not as a separate cause of action). The fraudulent inducement claim is framed on an independent factual basis (the pre-signing misrepresentation to induce contract execution) and paragraph 99 explicitly states it 'rests on Lumenara's fraudulent inducement of the JDA and the resulting injury to Vantage' and that it is 'independent of, and not limited to, the misappropriation of trade secrets,' with a further note that 'to the extent any part of this Count is found to rest on the same facts as Vantage's trade secret claims, it is pleaded in the alternative.' This language directly addresses the TUTSA preemption concern for the fraudulent inducement claim by framing it on an independent factual basis and adding alternative pleading language. The breach of contract claims are similarly framed on contractual obligations independent of trade secret law. The criterion asks whether TUTSA preemption is addressed 'in some manner' — the document does this through the independent factual basis framing and the explicit alternative pleading language in Count VI, satisfying the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Prayer: Compensatory Damages — Wasted Development Costs ($3.4M)
criteria_results.reasoning: The prayer for relief in Section VII, paragraph B explicitly states: 'and, in the alternative, reliance damages of approximately $3.4 million in wasted Project Meridian expenditures.' This directly identifies the $3.4M wasted development costs as a component of the compensatory damages requested. Additionally, paragraph 61 in Count I also references 'reliance damages equal to the approximately $3.4 million in engineering and technical resources Vantage expended on Project Meridian, which Lumenara's non-performance rendered valueless.'

criteria_results.title: Prayer: Compensatory Damages — Lost Northfield Opportunity ($8.7M)
criteria_results.reasoning: The prayer for relief in Section VII, paragraph B explicitly requests 'Vantage's lost profits, including from the loss of the Northfield contract.' Additionally, paragraph 62 in Count I describes the Northfield Aerospace Solutions contract as having 'a total value of approximately $8.7 million' and alleges it as a component of compensatory damages. The prayer incorporates this by reference through the lost profits request tied to the Northfield contract. The $8.7M Northfield opportunity is identified in the damages allegations and referenced in the prayer for relief.

criteria_results.title: Prayer: Compensatory Damages — IP Misappropriation / Reasonable Royalty ($5.7M)
criteria_results.reasoning: The prayer for relief in the agent's output requests compensatory damages including 'actual loss and Lumenara's unjust enrichment from the misappropriation or, in the alternative, a reasonable royalty' (Prayer ¶ B), and patent damages 'in no event less than a reasonable royalty' (Prayer ¶ C). However, nowhere in the prayer or damages allegations is a specific figure of approximately $5.7 million identified for IP misappropriation or reasonable royalty damages. The only specific dollar figures mentioned are the ~$3.4 million in reliance damages, the ~$8.7 million Northfield contract, the ~$14.2 million LumiSense 400 revenue, and the ~$3.5 million monthly revenue rate. No $5.7 million figure appears anywhere in the document.

criteria_results.title: Prayer: Compensatory Damages — Total Approximately $18M
criteria_results.reasoning: The prayer for relief in the agent's output does not specify a total compensatory damages figure of approximately $18,087,500, nor does it itemize components that sum to that amount. Instead, it requests compensatory damages 'in an amount to be proven at trial' and mentions specific items like the Northfield contract loss (~$8.7M), reliance damages (~$3.4M), and LumiSense 400 revenues (~$14.2M through June 2024 plus ~$3.5M/month ongoing), but never aggregates these into a total of approximately $18,087,500 or any specific quantified total. The prayer is largely unquantified and open-ended, failing to meet the criterion of requesting approximately $18,087,500 in total compensatory damages or itemizing components summing to that amount.

criteria_results.title: Prayer: Injunctive Relief (ISSUE_009)
criteria_results.reasoning: The prayer for relief in Section VII, item G explicitly requests preliminary and permanent injunctive relief enjoining Lumenara from '(ii) making, using, selling, offering to sell, importing, or distributing the LumiSense 400 or any other product embodying or derived from them or infringing the '567 Patent.' This directly addresses enjoining Lumenara from continuing to manufacture, sell, or distribute the LumiSense 400, which incorporates Vantage's SensorCore™ technology.

criteria_results.title: Injunctive Relief: Irreparable Harm Alleged (ISSUE_009)
criteria_results.reasoning: The counterclaim explicitly alleges irreparable harm and inadequacy of monetary damages in multiple places: Count II (¶69) states Lumenara's breaches 'are continuing and have caused and will continue to cause Vantage irreparable harm for which damages are inadequate'; Count III (¶74) states breaches 'are continuing and are causing irreparable harm'; Count IV (¶84) seeks injunction to 'prevent any actual or threatened misappropriation'; Count VII (¶106) states infringement 'has caused and will continue to cause Vantage irreparable harm, including loss of exclusivity in a patented architecture and competition from its own design, for which there is no adequate remedy at law.' These allegations clearly satisfy the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Prayer: Exemplary/Punitive Damages (ISSUE_010)
criteria_results.reasoning: The prayer for relief explicitly requests exemplary damages in multiple places: (D) requests exemplary damages under 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(C) and Texas Civil Practice and Remedies Code § 134A.004(b) for trade secret misappropriation; (F) requests exemplary damages for fraud under Texas Civil Practice and Remedies Code § 41.003. The body of the counterclaim also alleges willful and malicious conduct throughout. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Prayer: Enhanced DTSA Damages (ISSUE_010)
criteria_results.reasoning: The prayer for relief explicitly requests 'Exemplary damages of up to two times Vantage's trade secret damages under 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(C)' (paragraph D). Additionally, Count IV (DTSA) at paragraph 83 explicitly states 'Vantage is therefore entitled to exemplary damages of up to two times its damages award under 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(C).' Both the DTSA count and the prayer for relief request enhanced damages for willful and malicious misappropriation under 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(C).

criteria_results.title: Prayer: Attorney's Fees Under DTSA (ISSUE_011)
criteria_results.reasoning: The prayer for relief in section J explicitly requests 'Reasonable attorneys' fees, expert witness fees, consulting fees, and costs under JDA § 13.5, JDA § 12.1, 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(D), Texas Civil Practice and Remedies Code §§ 38.001(b)(8) and 134A.005, and 35 U.S.C. § 285.' This directly cites 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(D), the DTSA fee-shifting provision. Additionally, paragraph 83 in Count IV explicitly states 'Vantage is therefore entitled to exemplary damages of up to two times its damages award under 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(C), and to its reasonable attorneys' fees under 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(D).' The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Prayer: Attorney's Fees Under Texas Law (ISSUE_011)
criteria_results.reasoning: The prayer for relief in Section J explicitly requests 'Reasonable attorneys' fees, expert witness fees, consulting fees, and costs under JDA § 13.5, JDA § 12.1, 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(D), Texas Civil Practice and Remedies Code §§ 38.001(b)(8) and 134A.005, and 35 U.S.C. § 285.' This directly invokes Texas Civil Practice and Remedies Code § 38.001(b)(8) as a basis for attorney's fees on the contract claims. Additionally, Counts I, II, and III each individually reference § 38.001(b)(8) as an alternative basis for fees. The criterion is clearly satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Prayer: Pre- and/or Post-Judgment Interest
criteria_results.reasoning: The prayer for relief in Section VII, item L explicitly requests 'Pre-judgment and post-judgment interest at the maximum rates allowed by law.' This satisfies the criterion requiring that the prayer request pre-judgment interest, post-judgment interest, or both.

criteria_results.title: Distractor: Correctly Treats SensorCore™ as Background IP, Not Foreground IP (DISTRACTOR_002)
criteria_results.reasoning: The counterclaim consistently and correctly characterizes SensorCore™ as Vantage's pre-existing Background IP. Paragraph 30 explicitly states that Vantage's Background IP includes 'its proprietary substrate-level sensor array designs, including all lithographic mask layouts, doping profiles, thermal management schematics, and related design data,' that 'Background IP remains the sole property of the owning party (JDA § 7.1),' and that 'Foreground IP...does not include any Background IP of either Party (JDA §§ 1.6, 7.2). The SensorCore™ architecture predates the JDA and was not jointly developed. It is Vantage's Background IP.' Multiple other paragraphs (15, 65, 66, 80, 103) reinforce this characterization. The document never suggests SensorCore™ is jointly owned Foreground IP.

criteria_results.title: Wasted Development Costs Accurately Stated ($3.4M)
criteria_results.reasoning: The counterclaim repeatedly and consistently states the wasted development costs as approximately $3.4 million. In paragraph 61, it states 'reliance damages equal to the approximately $3.4 million in engineering and technical resources Vantage expended on Project Meridian.' In paragraph 37, it states 'committing engineering resources to Project Meridian at the contractual rate of approximately $1.7 million per year, or approximately $3.4 million in total.' In paragraph 97, it references 'its out-of-pocket expenditure of approximately $3.4 million in Project Meridian resources.' In the Prayer for Relief section B, it states 'reliance damages of approximately $3.4 million in wasted Project Meridian expenditures.' The figure is consistently and accurately stated as $3.4M throughout the document.

criteria_results.title: Reasonable Royalty Damages Accurately Stated ($5.7M)
criteria_results.reasoning: The counterclaim mentions $14.2M in LumiSense 400 revenue and references reasonable royalty as a damages measure, but it never states a specific $5.7M figure or describes a 40% royalty rate calculation. The damages sections (Counts II, III, IV, V, and the Prayer) simply say damages will be proven at trial and reference reasonable royalty as an alternative measure, without specifying any dollar amount or royalty rate that would yield $5.7M. The criterion requires the counterclaim to state approximately $5.7M or describe the 40% × $14.2M calculation, neither of which appears in the document.

criteria_results.title: Expert/Investigation Costs Stated ($287,500)
criteria_results.reasoning: The counterclaim does not mention expert or investigation costs of approximately $287,500, nor does it itemize Ridgeline at $175,000 and Hawksmere Ventures at $112,500. While the document references Dr. Franklin Ayers of Ridgeline Technical Consulting LLC performing a teardown analysis and mentions attorneys' fees, expert witness fees, consulting fees, and costs in the prayer for relief, no specific dollar amounts for expert or investigation costs are quantified anywhere in the document.

criteria_results.title: Factual Background: Bellingham-DeLuca Emails Pre-Date JDA Execution
criteria_results.reasoning: The counterclaim clearly establishes the temporal relationship between the Bellingham-DeLuca emails and the JDA execution. Paragraph 23 states the Bellingham email was sent on 'Sunday, May 15, 2022, at 4:47 p.m. PDT' and paragraph 25 states DeLuca replied on 'Monday, May 16, 2022.' Paragraph 28 then states the JDA was executed 'On June 1, 2022' and explicitly notes that 'Mr. DeLuca signed for Lumenara, fifteen days after writing the May 16, 2022 email.' The fraudulent inducement count (paragraph 94) also references that the emails were sent 'Fifteen and sixteen days earlier' before the JDA signing. This makes the temporal relationship unmistakably clear.

criteria_results.title: DTSA Count References Willful/Malicious Conduct
criteria_results.reasoning: Count IV (DTSA) at paragraph 83 explicitly states: 'Lumenara's misappropriation was willful and malicious. Its CEO and Program Manager planned it in writing before the JDA was signed. They kept the plan "close-hold" to avoid alerting Vantage and carried it out despite express acknowledgment that the JDA protected Vantage's Background IP. Vantage is therefore entitled to exemplary damages of up to two times its damages award under 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(C), and to its reasonable attorneys' fees under 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(D).' This directly satisfies the criterion requiring willful and malicious characterization in the DTSA count to support enhanced damages and attorney's fees.

criteria_results.title: Factual Background: CES Announcement and Commercial Launch Dates
criteria_results.reasoning: The document explicitly mentions both dates. Paragraph 47 states 'On January 8, 2024, 27 days after Ms. Vasquez's final download, Lumenara announced the LumiSense 400 at CES.' Paragraph 49 states 'Lumenara began commercial sales of the LumiSense 400 on March 1, 2024.' Both the CES announcement date and the commercial launch date are clearly referenced in the factual allegations.

criteria_results.title: Rule 9(b) Compliance: Fraudulent Inducement Pleads Named Individuals
criteria_results.reasoning: Count VI (Fraudulent Inducement) explicitly names Martin DeLuca (Lumenara's CEO) as the individual who made the written representations in Section 9.3 of the JDA on June 1, 2022, and also references Craig Bellingham (Program Manager) as the person who sent the May 15 email outlining the scheme. The count identifies DeLuca by name as the signatory who executed the JDA and made the false representations, satisfying Rule 9(b)'s requirement to identify named individuals who made or directed the misrepresentations.

criteria_results.title: Rule 9(b) Compliance: Fraudulent Inducement Pleads Approximate Dates
criteria_results.reasoning: Count VI (Fraudulent Inducement) includes specific dates for the misrepresentations. Paragraph 93 states the representations were made 'On June 1, 2022' in Section 9.3 of the JDA. Paragraph 94 references the emails from 'Fifteen and sixteen days earlier' (i.e., May 15-16, 2022), which are also specifically dated in paragraphs 23-26. The count clearly identifies when the fraudulent conduct occurred with specific dates.

criteria_results.title: Rule 9(b) Compliance: Fraudulent Inducement Pleads Substance of Misrepresentation
criteria_results.reasoning: Count VI (Fraudulent Inducement) at paragraphs 91-99 clearly describes the substance of the misrepresentations: specifically, the written representations in JDA Section 9.3 that Lumenara was 'entering into this Agreement in good faith and with the genuine intent to perform its obligations' and that it 'has no present intention or plan to use the collaboration...for any purpose other than the Project.' The count also identifies who made the representations (CEO Martin DeLuca), when (June 1, 2022, upon executing the JDA), and why they were false (citing the May 15-16, 2022 emails showing the actual intent to 'extract' SensorCore technology). This satisfies Rule 9(b)'s requirement to plead the who, what, when, where, and how of the alleged fraud, and specifically describes the substance of what was misrepresented.

criteria_results.title: Rule 9(b) Compliance: Fraudulent Inducement Pleads Resulting Harm
criteria_results.reasoning: Count VI (Fraudulent Inducement) at paragraph 97 explicitly alleges harm resulting from the misrepresentations: 'As a direct and proximate result, Vantage has suffered damages in an amount to be proven at trial. These include its out-of-pocket expenditure of approximately $3.4 million in Project Meridian resources, the loss of the Northfield contract, and the harm from Lumenara's exploitation of the SensorCore™ technology that Vantage disclosed in reliance on Lumenara's representations.' This clearly satisfies the requirement that the fraudulent inducement count allege how Vantage was harmed by the misrepresentations.

criteria_results.title: Demand for Jury Trial
criteria_results.reasoning: Section VI of the counterclaim is titled 'JURY TRIAL' and explicitly addresses the jury trial issue. It states that Vantage 'demands a trial by jury on it under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 38' to the extent any issue is not subject to the contractual jury waiver. This constitutes a jury trial demand within the body of the document.
